strengths: Well-motivated approach: Addressing the asymmetry between single visual representations and hierarchical textual representations in vision-language models for taxonomic classification is an intuitive and important problem.

Sound and creative mathematical formulation: Embedding each modality into a hyperbolic manifold with separate learnable curvatures, deriving an analytic surrogate for KL divergence between wrapped normal distributions, and solving for an optimal intermediate bridging manifold via the Implicit Function Theorem is technically elegant and well-developed.
Solid theoretical support: The authors provide formal proofs for the existence, uniqueness, and monotonicity of the intermediate curvature minimizer under clearly specified conditions.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Extensive experiments across four benchmarks (CIFAR-100, SUN, ImageNet, Rare Species) and various regimes (few-shot, base-to-novel generalization) show consistent and significant improvements, particularly on Hierarchical Consistent Accuracy (HCA).

Thorough ablation studies and diagnostics: The paper includes meaningful ablations covering the feature extraction module, hyperbolic geometric constraints, distance formulations, curvature dynamics, computational efficiency, and attention/representation visualizations.
weaknesses: The theoretical derivation of the manifold distance relies on multiple approximations, including a first-order Taylor expansion around a numerically solved point and an assumption of a constant feature midpoint norm r in the tangent space.

The visual tree feature extraction mechanism conditions the visual features on textual features via cross-attention (Eq. 5), which makes visual feature computation dependent on the text query candidates, potentially complicating inference scalability when candidate label spaces are very large or dynamically changing.

While the overall gains over the Euclidean/flat baselines are substantial, the incremental gain brought specifically by the intermediate manifold search over simpler hyperbolic variants (e.g., Ours-HypV1 with shared curvature or Ours-HypV2 with independent curvatures without intermediate bridging) is relatively moderate in several benchmark settings.

strengths: Addresses an important and recognized problem in multimodal hierarchy learning: the structural asymmetry between fine-grained hierarchical text taxonomies and standard single visual representations.

Proposes a well-motivated and mathematically principled framework for heterogeneous hyperbolic manifold alignment, deriving an intermediate manifold via an approximated KL divergence between wrapped normal distributions with theoretical guarantees of existence and uniqueness.
Cleverly handles the non-differentiable line-search solver (golden section search) using the implicit function theorem to allow end-to-end gradient updates for individual manifold curvatures.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation on Taxonomic Open Set classification across multiple benchmarks (Cifar-100, SUN, ImageNet, Rare Species) demonstrating consistent and significant gains in hierarchical metrics (HCA and MTA) over both Euclidean prompt-tuning baselines (MaPLe, PromptSRC, ProTeCt) and hyperbolic baselines (MERU, HyCoCLIP).

Thorough ablation studies, sensitivity analyses, clustering metric evaluations, runtime overhead analyses, and qualitative visualizations (attention maps across taxonomic levels) that support the design choices.
weaknesses: The manifold distance metric derivation relies on several heuristic approximations, including a first-order Taylor expansion around a fixed empirical scalar point and assuming the feature midpoint norm is constant/estimated per batch.

The approach requires explicit, well-defined hierarchical label structures (such as biological or WordNet taxonomies), limiting its direct applicability to general open-vocabulary vision-language tasks where category relationships are unstructured or continuous.

The overall pipeline has considerable engineering complexity, combining intermediate class-token routing with suppressed self-attention, cross-attention feature extraction, multi-curvature hyperbolic embeddings, dynamic intermediate curvature search, implicit differentiation, and multiple cone-entailment losses.

A substantial portion of the performance gains appears to stem from the semantic-aware visual feature tree extraction itself (as seen from the Ours-Euc ablation), slightly tempering the standalone empirical contribution of the heterogeneous hyperbolic geometry.

strengths: Well-motivated formulation: The paper clearly identifies a fundamental limitation in existing hierarchical vision-language alignment methods, namely the structural asymmetry between multi-level textual hierarchies and single Euclidean image embeddings.

Technically sound heterogeneous manifold framework: Rather than forcing both modalities to share an identical curvature, the paper allows visual and textual spaces to maintain distinct learnable curvatures, formulating an optimal intermediate manifold via an information-theoretic distance surrogate and optimizing curvature parameters end-to-end via the implicit function theorem.

Rigorous theoretical analysis: The authors provide formal proofs for the existence and uniqueness of the optimal intermediate manifold curvature within the interval of modality curvatures under well-defined conditions.

Extensive and convincing experimental evaluation: The proposed method is thoroughly benchmarked across four datasets (CIFAR-100, SUN, ImageNet, Rare Species) under both few-shot and base-to-novel generalization settings, demonstrating consistent and substantial gains, especially in hierarchical consistency metrics (HCA and MTA) over strong baselines such as ProTeCt, MaPLe, and PromptSRC.

Thorough ablations and diagnostic analyses: The appendix provides extensive ablations verifying the contribution of each component (Euclidean vs. single curvature vs. heterogeneous curvatures, manifold distance definitions, cross-attention mechanism) as well as feature clustering metrics, efficiency benchmarks, and GradCAM visualizations.
weaknesses: Surrogate approximations in manifold distance: The derived manifold distance function $D_L(\mathcal{L}^{c_1}, \mathcal{L}^{c_3})$ relies on several approximations—specifically a first-order Taylor expansion of $\operatorname{arccosh}^2$ around an empirically chosen expansion point $y_1^* \approx 3.016$ and treating the tangent-space midpoint norm $r$ as a constant—meaning the objective is an engineered surrogate rather than an exact divergence between Riemannian manifolds.

Inference dependency on candidate textual hierarchies: The visual hierarchy extraction framework employs cross-attention with textual features acting as queries to produce hierarchy-specific visual tokens. At test time, this couples visual feature extraction with the set of candidate text labels/paths, which could add computational overhead in large-scale retrieval or open-vocabulary settings where candidate paths are numerous.

Modest leaf accuracy improvements on certain benchmarks: While the method yields dramatic improvements on hierarchical consistency metrics (HCA and MTA), the improvements on flat Leaf Accuracy (LA) are relatively incremental in several settings (e.g., SUN 1-shot with PromptSRC improves from 70.61% to 70.64%).

Scope limited to taxonomic open-set classification: The experimental validation is strictly confined to tree-structured taxonomic benchmarks; evaluating the applicability of the heterogeneous manifold alignment to broader open-vocabulary vision-language tasks without explicit pre-defined hierarchies would strengthen the impact.

strengths: Well-motivated formulation: The paper clearly identifies the asymmetry between hierarchical textual semantics and flat visual features in existing vision-language models, presenting an intuitive tree-to-tree alignment paradigm.

Solid technical formulation: The authors propose embedding textual and visual feature trees into distinct hyperbolic manifolds with learnable curvatures, formulating an intermediate manifold search via wrapped normal KL-divergence minimization and utilizing the implicit function theorem for end-to-end optimization.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The approach achieves consistent and noticeable gains across four datasets (CIFAR-100, SUN, ImageNet, and Rare Species) in both few-shot and base-to-novel generalization settings, notably outperforming state-of-the-art hierarchical prompt tuning (ProTeCt) and hyperbolic baselines (MERU, HyCoCLIP) on hierarchical consistency metrics (HCA, MTA).

Insightful qualitative analysis: The GradCAM visualizations across taxonomic levels demonstrate that the model effectively attends to semantically meaningful visual attributes corresponding to the respective level of taxonomy (coarse vs. fine-grained).
weaknesses: Mathematical rigor of Theorem 1: The derivation of the manifold distance in Eq. (9) / Theorem 1 relies on a first-order Taylor expansion around an empirically/numerically chosen expansion point ($y_1^* \approx 3.016$) to ensure vanishing derivative at $c_3=c_1$. Calling this an affine transformation of the KL divergence is somewhat misleading, as it is a heuristic local surrogate approximation rather than a closed-form derivation of the actual KL divergence.

Missing runtime and computational complexity analysis: The training loop (Algorithm 2) requires running a Golden Section Search to find $c_3^*$ followed by second-derivative implicit gradient computations at every training iteration. The paper does not report training overhead, wall-clock time, or convergence behavior compared to baseline methods like MaPLe or ProTeCt.

Sensitivity to architecture choices: The selection of intermediate layers (fixed to layers 4 and 7 for ViT-B/16) is not ablated. It remains unclear how sensitive the performance and tree structure are to the depth and number of sampled intermediate ViT layers.

Minor typos and presentation errors: Section 2 heading is misspelled as 'REALTED WORKS'; Eq. (18) contains an error in the update rule ($c_2 \leftarrow c_1 - \eta \cdot \frac{dJ}{dc_1}$ instead of $c_2 \leftarrow c_2 - \eta \cdot \frac{dJ}{dc_2}$); and Appendix C.3 contains a LaTeX compilation typo ('textitasizes' instead of 'emphasizes').

strengths: Clear motivation and well-formulated problem: addressing the asymmetry between single visual representations and multi-level hierarchical text representations in vision-language models for taxonomic classification.

Sound and mathematically rigorous framework: formulating heterogeneous hyperbolic manifold alignment via an affine transformation of KL divergence between wrapped normal distributions, proving the existence and uniqueness of the optimal intermediate manifold curvature, and leveraging the implicit function theorem (IFT) for end-to-end gradient backpropagation.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: validates on four benchmark datasets (CIFAR-100, SUN, ImageNet, and Rare Species) across few-shot and base-to-novel generalization settings, achieving significant improvements in Hierarchical Consistent Accuracy (HCA) and Mean Treecut Accuracy (MTA) over strong baselines (ProTeCt, MaPLe, PromptSRC, MERU, HyCoCLIP).

Thorough ablations and insightful visualizations: progressive ablations clearly demonstrate the individual benefits of the multi-layer visual feature extraction, hyperbolic embedding, and heterogeneous intermediate manifold search. Grad-CAM and t-SNE visualizations convincingly demonstrate coarse-to-fine semantic grounding.
weaknesses: Approximation assumptions in Theorem 1 and Propositions 1-2: the derivation relies on a first-order Taylor expansion around an empirically solved anchor point ($y_1^* \approx 3.016$) and treats the tangent midpoint norm $r = \|\bar{v}\|$ as a constant under lower-bound conditions ($r \ge r_{\min}$). Further discussion on the empirical stability and sensitivity to these approximations in practice would strengthen the theoretical contribution.

Inference dependence and computational complexity: visual features are constructed via cross-attention conditioned on textual hierarchy embeddings as queries. The paper does not report training/inference latency or memory overhead introduced by the golden section search, implicit gradient computations, and query-dependent visual feature extraction.

Minor notation and typographical errors: for example, in Section 2, the section heading contains a typo ('REALTED WORKS'); in Eq. (18), the update rule for $c_2$ incorrectly writes $c_2 \leftarrow c_1 - \eta \cdot \frac{dJ}{dc_1}$ instead of $c_2 \leftarrow c_2 - \eta \cdot \frac{dJ}{dc_2}$.

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: Standard vision-language alignment maps a single global image embedding to hierarchical text labels, creating an inherent structural asymmetry. Extracting multi-level visual features to build symmetric image-text feature trees directly addresses this limitation.

Principled geometric modeling: Accommodating different curvatures for visual and textual manifolds is geometrically well-founded since the modalities possess different semantic densities and structural granularities. Bridging them via an intermediate manifold using wrapped normal distribution approximations is mathematically creative.

Use of implicit differentiation: Applying the implicit function theorem to differentiate through the 1D golden section search of the optimal intermediate curvature provides an elegant end-to-end training pipeline.

Strong and extensive experimental validation: The proposed method is evaluated across four benchmark datasets (CIFAR-100, SUN, ImageNet, and Rare Species) and multiple settings (few-shot, base-to-novel, base-to-whole). It demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over competitive baselines (e.g., ProTeCt, HyCoCLIP), particularly on hierarchical consistency metrics such as HCA and MTA.
weaknesses: Heuristic assumptions in the theoretical derivations: In Appendix A.1 (Theorem 1), the KL divergence approximation relies on a first-order Taylor expansion around an empirically chosen point ($y_1^* \approx 3.016$), and treats $r = \|\bar{v}\|$ as a constant even though tangent-space embeddings evolve during training. Furthermore, the uniqueness and convexity results in Propositions 1 and 2 require $r$ to exceed a threshold $r_{\min}$, but the paper does not clarify whether or how this condition is enforced or monitored during actual model training.

Computational overhead and scalability: The method requires performing a 1D golden section search and computing second-order derivatives via the implicit function theorem at every training iteration, alongside carrying intermediate ViT tokens through subsequent transformer blocks. The paper lacks runtime and memory benchmarking relative to standard prompt-tuning baselines.

Sensitivity and architectural choices: The choice of intermediate ViT layers (specifically the 4th and 7th layers) appears heuristic and is specific to ViT-B/16. An ablation or sensitivity analysis on layer selection and key hyperparameters (e.g., cone aperture constant $k$, entailment weight $\alpha$) is missing.

Typographical and notation errors: There is a notable typo in the update rule in Eq. (18), which writes '$c_2 \leftarrow c_1 - \eta \cdot \frac{dJ}{dc_1}$' instead of updating $c_2$ with respect to its own gradient. In addition, the Section 2 title contains an obvious misspelling ('REALTED WORKS').
